summary: Summation No. 20 covers May 1947 (with much economic data for March-April), the month the new Constitution took effect on 3 May and the first Diet under it met on 20 May. After a month of interparty bargaining, Social Democrat Tetsu Katayama was named Prime Minister on 24 May and a three-party Cabinet was announced on 29 May. SCAP created a Reparations Section and a Reparations Technical Advisory Committee. The report details the Tokyo war crimes tribunal's defense case (China and Russian phases), Japanese judicial reform, and war crimes trials. Economic chapters cover record coke, steel and housing output, textile recovery, coal shortfalls, the abolition of the 700-yen wage limit, rationing, imports, finance and property control. Social chapters report health statistics, repatriation, teacher screening, religion and media. A historian will find dense monthly statistics and charts for tracking Occupation-era recovery.
highlights: Japan's new Constitution took effect on 3 May, and MacArthur restored the national flag for display over the Diet, Supreme Court, Prime Minister's premises and the Emperor's residence.

The first Diet under the Constitution met 20 May: Tsuneo Matsudaira became President of the House of Councillors, Komakichi Matsuoka Speaker of the House of Representatives, and the Ryokufu Kai formed with 90 members.

Social Democrat Tetsu Katayama was designated Prime Minister on 24 May by 420 to 6 in the lower house; after Liberal talks failed, a three-party Cabinet of eight Social Democrats, seven Democrats and two People's Cooperatives was announced 29 May.
General Orders No. 8 (8 May) created the SCAP Reparations Section and No. 9 (21 May) the Reparations Technical Advisory Committee; ten nations had reparations delegations in Japan.
At the Tokyo tribunal the defense finished the China Phase on 16 May and opened the Russian Phase, disputing responsibility for the Panay bombing and denying knowledge of Nanking atrocities.
April fish catch rose to five times March's on the herring run, while coal output in the first 20 days of May was 1,244,600 tons, 103,600 below the same April period.
The 700-yen wage and salary limit under the Emergency Financial Measures was abolished 1 May, and Bank of Japan notes in circulation reached 129,685,000,000 yen on 31 May.
Imperial ordinances created a Labor Standards Bureau in the Ministry of Welfare; about 400,000 workers attended Tokyo's quiet May Day; repatriates from 28 April to 31 May numbered about 69,700.

sections.title: Front matter
sections.summary: Cover for Summation No. 20 (May 1947), table of contents by part and section, and the list of 104 charts, maps and graphs.

sections.title: Part I: General
sections.summary: Monthly digest: SCAP created reparations bodies, Constitution Day passed and the Katayama Cabinet formed, with economic gains and shortages and health, education and media news.

sections.title: Organization Under SCAP
sections.summary: General Orders No. 8 (8 May) created the Reparations Section; No. 9 (21 May) set up the Reparations Technical Advisory Committee.

sections.title: Political Activities
sections.summary: Constitution Day on 3 May, new Diet officers, Katayama's selection as Prime Minister on 24 May, the three-party Cabinet, public safety figures and war crimes trials.

sections.title: Economic Activities
sections.summary: Herring-run fish surge, coal and log trends, record coke and steel output, textile expansion, labor ordinances, rationing, finance and property control, with production index charts.

sections.title: Social Activities
sections.summary: Health officials' meetings, National Institute of Health dedication on 21 May, 3,181 hospitals, teacher dismissals, religious conventions, Constitution Week and library attendance of 15,421.

sections.title: Part II: Political
sections.summary: Constitution, Diet and May Cabinet crisis, public safety statistics, Japanese judicial reform, and the Tokyo tribunal's China and Russian defense phases.

sections.title: Government and Politics
sections.summary: Constitution Day, Diet organization, the May Cabinet crisis ending in Katayama's election and a three-party Cabinet, party developments, neighborhood associations and the purge.

sections.title: Public Safety
sections.summary: Crime rose from 129,440 to 154,874 offenses in March; 134 were killed in April rail accidents; prison deaths ran 1.6 per 1,000; 2,107 fires in March.

sections.title: Legal and War Crimes
sections.summary: Provisional laws revised the courts, arrest rules and Civil Code; 90 suspects ordered arrested; 21 trials of 34 defendants; tribunal testimony in the China and Russian phases.

sections.title: Part III: Economic
sections.summary: Production, transport, communications, labor, trade, rationing, finance and property control, with statistical charts for March and April 1947, including record coke, steel and housing output.

sections.title: Agriculture and Fisheries
sections.summary: Land reform progress; April fish catch five times March's on a herring run, gaining 357,017 metric tons; rope, salt and petroleum allocations.

sections.title: Forestry and Mining
sections.summary: April log output fell 88,688,000 board feet to 646,340,000; coal output slipped in May; lignite, oil drilling and mineral output also covered.

sections.title: Heavy Industries
sections.summary: Coke at a 1946-47 high, postwar-high iron and steel, ferroalloys nearly doubled, housing peak of about 43,000 structures, plus chemicals, machine tools and machinery.

sections.title: Manufacturing
sections.summary: April output: flour milling up 70.5 percent in March on cereal imports; tin plate shortage cut can production; truck chassis fell to 643 against 869; watch and clock output hit a postwar high of 123,406.

sections.title: Textile Industries
sections.summary: Textile output kept rising from February through April in all branches except raw silk reeling, across cotton, silk, rayon, wool and knit goods.

sections.title: Transportation and Public Utilities
sections.summary: April operable trucks rose to 51,378 and buses to 7,604; railways carried 278,163,667 passengers; power generation reached 2,728,180,000 kWh, up 12.2 percent; gas output averaged 1,209,210 cubic meters daily.

sections.title: Communications
sections.summary: International Telecommunications Company liquidated 25 May, Ministry of Communications paying $1,200,000 monthly rent; telephone and telegraph traffic hit peaks; Osaka-Colombo radiotelegraph circuit opened 10 May; 75 research laboratories counted.

sections.title: Labor
sections.summary: Imperial ordinances created the Labor Standards Bureau; May Day drew 400,000 in Tokyo; disputes idled .19 percent of working time; union conventions and employment covered.

sections.title: Imports and Exports
sections.summary: Imports by commodity group (food, textiles, machinery, chemicals, metals, wood) and exports including 15,425,000 linear yards of cotton fabric shipped to five countries.

sections.title: Rationing and Price Control
sections.summary: Rice collections reached 4,222,100 tons since 30 September; imports made up 30 percent of the May ration; fertilizer deliveries, price increases and violations reported.

sections.title: Finance
sections.summary: The 700-yen wage ceiling was abolished 1 May; note circulation hit 129,685,000,000 yen; Capital Levy collections reached 16,650,000,000 yen; banks, deposit bureau and liquidation covered.

sections.title: Property Control and Reparations
sections.summary: 278 looted ships reported; allied and war-criminal property, German patents, zaibatsu holding company shares, rehabilitation expenditures, and reparations delegations of ten nations.

sections.title: Part IV: Social
sections.summary: Public health, welfare and repatriation, followed by education, religion, arts and media, ending with a map of Japan.

sections.title: Public Health and Welfare
sections.summary: Communicable disease rates, veterinary affairs, hospitals, medical supplies, narcotics, relief to 2,763,041 persons, social security and repatriation from Soviet areas.

sections.title: Education, Religion and Media of Expression
sections.summary: Teacher screening committees (120,000 teachers gone), religious conventions, cultural sites, radio, press, films with 475,637 attendance, theater, music, library, and a map of Japan.
